The real purpose of the digital transformation is not simply to digitalize government, it's to change the relationship between the citizens and the state. For decades, governments have been organized around institutions, administrative boundaries, but the people do not live their lives through institutions. They experience life through the events, the needs, and moments. The true opportunity of technology is to make governments adapt to people's lives rather than requiring people to adapt to government processes. That is why we believe that the next stage of the EA-native government, it's when not government that simply automate existing processes processes, but governments that become more responsive, more proactive, and more human-centered. For the last two decades, we have been building digital states. Perhaps the next decade should be about connecting them. Today, data, documents, and digital services often stop at the national borders, even though people, businesses, trade, and ideas do not. If we can build trusted digital bridges between countries, we can reduce frictions, accelerate economic cooperation, facilitate mobility, and make public services more accessible across borders. In this sense, the future of the digital transformation, it's not only about connecting people to the digital world. It's maybe— it's also be about connecting digital states to one another. I guess that's why we're having the conversation. The reality is that African countries, for instance, continue to struggle with a set of common, yet often invisible challenges. The challenges of trust, for instance, which is really key in everything we're talking about, but also coordination and knowledge. And these frictions turn into invisible costs that are borne by everyday citizens. Imagine that we have over 500 million— if we have over 500 million people who lack a verifiable identity, It means every basic transaction will stall. It means that they cannot access credit. They cannot save. They cannot access insurance or the services that they are owed. So that is, for us, a development silencer. When public service delivery operates in paper-based, donor-funded silos, coordination becomes painful. Painfully slow and quite leaky, wasting the very resources that we need at a moment when development financing is also declining and every dollar must count. It becomes a structural barrier that's keeping ordinary entrepreneurs and small businesses locked out of their own digital economy. Our analysis shows that the single biggest blocker to achieving this vision, actually achieving it at scale, is not the lack of political will, as we've heard every government that's spoken. The will is there. It's the lack of structural financing and innovative financing, but also investment-ready national projects, and that's where we come in. This week, we're excited to be launching a new initiative which is our Africa Accelerator for DPI, and the idea here is really to work with countries over the next 18 months in an intensive partnership that's timed to the global review and in creating a platform, and the platform will provide a structured pathway for digital readiness diagnostics, It will mobilize specialized technical expertise and actively build the pipelines of investment-ready projects that are required to unlock available sovereign and concessional finance. Everyone says capital is not the issue, it's not the problem, it exists, but how do we unlock it for initiatives like this? These are not pilots anymore. The infrastructure of the future is being built right now, and I think We have to make sure it is built right, but also we have to make sure that it's built for everyone.
